document.title: Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. in response to FERC's 07/30/2026 Notice re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
       
PJM Governance and Stakeholder 
Reforms 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
COMMENTS OF BUCKEYE POWER, INC. 
 
Buckeye Power, Inc. (“Buckeye”) submits these comments pursuant to the 
Commission’s Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment of July 30, 2026.1  
Buckeye is an Ohio non-profit generation and transmission cooperative that 
produces, procures, and provides at wholesale all the electric capacity, energy, and 
transmission required by its member electric distribution cooperatives. Buckeye operates 
as a cooperative and is owned by its 25 member distribution cooperatives, which are in 
turn each owned by their member-consumers.2  Those member cooperatives serve more 
than 400,000 residential, commercial, and industrial customers in service territories 
encompassing 77 of Ohio’s 88 counties. Buckeye operates not for the benefit of 
shareholders, but for the benefit of its member-consumers.  
 
1 Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment (July 30, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260730-3067 (the 
“Notice”). 
2 The 25 distribution cooperative members of Buckeye are: Adams Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; 
Buckeye Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Butler Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Carroll Electric 
Cooperative, Inc.; Consolidated Cooperative, Inc.; Darke Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Firelands 
Electric Cooperative, Inc.; The Frontier Power Company; Guernsey-Muskingum Electric Cooperative, Inc.; 
Hancock-Wood Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Holmes-Wayne Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Licking Rural 
Electrification, Inc.; Logan County Cooperative Power and Light Association, Inc.; Lorain-Medina Rural 
Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Mid-Ohio Energy Cooperative, Inc.; Midwest Electric, Inc.; Midwest Energy & 
Communications; North Central Electric Cooperative, Inc.; North Western Electric Cooperative, Inc.; 
Paulding-Putnam Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Pioneer Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; South Central Power 
Company; Tricounty Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; Union Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc.; and 
Washington Electric Cooperative, Inc.

- 2 - 
 
Buckeye’s mission is to provide “to all member systems, stably and competitively 
priced, economical and highly reliable wholesale power, for the benefit of their members 
and their communities.”3 Buckeye provides this supply through wholesale power 
agreements under which it obtains generation resources and transmission service to meet 
the demand of its members, and its members pay a cost-based rate for these resources. 
Buckeye or its affiliates own or have the right to the output of approximately 2,445 
megawatts of generating capacity located in or delivered into PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C. (“PJM”). Buckeye is both a taker of transmission service under the PJM Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and a participant in the PJM market. Buckeye 
participates in the PJM market both as a market seller (as a generation owner) and as a 
buyer (as a Load-Serving Entity). 
Buckeye has appended to these comments its responses to the questions posed in 
the appendix to the Notice.  
Respectfully submitted, 
 
/s/ Lija Kaleps-Clark___ 
Kurt P. Helfrich

3 Buckeye’s mission statement can be found on its website at https://ohioec.org/buckeye-power.

Questions/Comments 
Yes 
No 
1) 
Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
Y 
  
  
Comments:  
2) 
Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member may serve (e.g., 10 years)? 
Y 
 
  
Comments:  
3) 
Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a preference for some Board 
members that reside in the PJM region? 
Y 
  
  
Comments: Buckeye is supportive of giving “preference” for Board members that reside in the PJM 
region.  However, residence within PJM should not be a requirement for Board member qualification as this 
would likely limit the number of qualified candidates. 
4) 
Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling off period for Board 
members from two years to one year? 
Y 
  
  
Comments:  
5) 
Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable more communication between 
the Board and stakeholders? 
  
N

- 4 - 
 
  
Comments:  Existing processes allow multiple opportunities for the Board and the stakeholders to 
communicate.  Relaxing restrictions is not necessary and may lead to unrestricted ex parte communications and 
undermine independent decision-making. 
6) 
In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public or the Board be required to 
explain its reasoning? 
Y 
  
  
Comments:  
7) 
In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open or available to the 
public? 
Y  
 
  
Comments: Buckeye supports allowing certain Board meetings to be open to the public, recognizing the value of 
transparency and stakeholder engagement. However, Buckeye does not support requiring all Board meetings to 
be open to the public, as non-public meetings can provide an important forum for candid, open discussion, 
deliberation, and the exchange of ideas that supports effective decision-making. 
8) 
Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that the responsibility of PJM 
and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
Y 
 
  
Comments: 
9) 
Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the Nominating Committee? 
Y 
 
  
Comments:

- 5 - 
 
10) 
Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management compensation to their 
achievement? 
  
N 
  
Comments:  
11) 
Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only inform the Board? 
  
N 
  
Comments: While Buckeye agrees with the ability for PJM to have Section 205 filing rights as indicated in 
response to questions 12 and 13 below, Buckeye believes the stakeholder process is important and valuable to 
identify the most effective solutions.  Buckeye thus supports PJM stakeholders having “jump ball” rights where 
PJM has Section 205 filing rights when a supermajority of stakeholders approve an alternative proposal as 
indicated in response to question 15.      
12) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the energy market and ancillary services 
unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds of the Members Committee? 
Y 
  
  
Comments: 
13) 
Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over Regional Transmission Expansion Planning 
(RTEP) unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds of the Members 
Committee? 
Y 
  
  
Comments:  
14) 
Should the Organization of PJM States Inc (OPSI) have “jump ball” rights over resource 
adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings when a supermajority of OPSI agrees on an 
alternative proposal? 
 
N 
  
Comments:

- 6 - 
 
15) 
Should the Members Committee have “jump ball” filing rights over the portions of the tariff 
where PJM has 205 filing rights when a supermajority of stakeholders approves an alternative 
proposal? 
Y 
 
 
Comments: 
16) 
Should the approval threshold in the Members Committee be lowered from two-thirds sector-
weighted voting? 
  
N 
  
Comments: 
17) 
Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which apply to senior standing committees, also 
apply to lower-level committees? 
Y 
  
  
Comments: 
 
18) 
In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state representative group consisting of governors’ 
representatives and/or state legislators’ representatives? 
Y 
 
  
Comments: Buckeye supports the creation of an additional state representative group if states determine that such 
a group is needed. 
19) 
Should state representatives have a formal voting role in the stakeholder process (limited to 
certain topics, such as resource adequacy and regional transmission cost allocation) in addition to 
the consumer advocate votes?  
Y 
 
  
Comments:

- 7 - 
 
20) 
Should PJM be required to consult with OPSI prior to making a section 205 filing related to 
resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation? 
Y
